source.title: Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic

record.tranche_reason: It tests whether narrow supervised fine-tuning can produce broadly misaligned behavior on unrelated prompts, using bad-advice fine-tunes and general-query evaluations. This is the same basic intervention and outcome as the claim, but in a different narrow-task setting.
record.gate_note: The paper also steers models toward evilness using explicitly evil training examples and evaluates sycophancy and refusal. Those induced behaviors do not count as spontaneous misalignment evidence for these claim versions. The bad-advice fine-tunes followed by general-query misalignment evaluations, and the weight-vector comparisons, are the relevant results.
record.test_reason: The paper's focus is a weight-steering and monitoring method. But §5 and App. I report its own emergent-misalignment results: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct fine-tuned on bad medical, financial or sports advice shows 11–31% EM on Betley-style general questions, versus 0% at baseline. It also reports onset during training and weight-space similarity to an 'evil' direction. That is a new setting with results on V2, V7 and (correlationally) V5. The sycophancy, evil-MCQA and refusal experiments induce behaviour by design and bear on no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The paper's main conclusion is that contrastive weight steering often generalises further than activation steering for sycophancy, evilness and refusal. On EM, the authors give 'preliminary evidence' that bad-advice fine-tune updates align more with an evil weight direction than with control directions. They suggest weight monitoring might detect misalignment, while calling the monitoring experiments narrow in scope.
record.recipe_differences: Uses narrow fine-tuning followed by evaluation on general prompts, but the narrow data are bad medical, financial, or sports advice rather than insecure code; it also investigates weight-vector monitoring rather than matched secure-code and classroom-request controls.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different results across bad-advice domains in aggregate, but does not assign the EM-rate range to individual domains. The sports fine-tune is the one for which an approximate emergence step is stated.

fits_no_version.finding: Cosine similarity between the model weights and the evil weight vectors rises during bad-sports fine-tuning, tracking EM onset. It does not rise for the Alpaca fine-tune.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight-space similarity to a contrastive evil direction can serve as a training-time monitor for emergent misalignment.

record.problems: The reported EM and coherence rates are ranges across fine-tunes, with no per-domain mapping in the text. No seed robustness analysis is reported. The shared-direction evidence is based on weight-vector similarities and does not establish causal mediation.

untested.parts: Harmless reward hacks and number sequences. EM of the good-advice counterpart fine-tunes is not reported.
Whether the direction causally mediates EM (no ablation or steering-away on the EM models). Activation-space or persona features.
Seed robustness, multiple model sizes, and explicit coherence-filter sensitivity.
Not tested on EM. The refusal and sycophancy mitigation experiments concern induced drift, not EM.

missing.what: Alpaca control fine-tune tracked through training shows EM near zero and no rise in cosine similarity to the evil vector, unlike bad sports advice.
Cosine similarities between raw task vectors (non-contrastive) do not group the bad-advice fine-tunes together.
Similarity of evil weight vectors to task vectors from the same domains.

record.verdict_notes: EM results are a validation step for the monitoring experiment, run on one model and one run per domain. The reader's linking of r2 as partial is changed to observed. The evil steering and refusal sections induce the behaviour deliberately and are excluded.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning or matched secure-code/class controls.
Tests bad-advice fine-tunes in medical, financial, and sports domains; does not test harmless reward hacks or number sequences.
No narrow in-context examples without fine-tuning.
Compares weight-vector similarities and reports a shared direction, but does not causally test whether that direction mediates misaligned behavior.
No inoculation framing or brief benign retraining to prevent or reverse emergent misalignment.

Reports bad-advice results and an approximate emergence point during training. Does not test seeds or compare open-model sizes; coherence is reported, but no separate seed robustness analysis is given.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on bad-advice datasets in medical, financial, and sports domains; evaluated on general queries.

conditions.value: bad advice: medical, financial, and sports

rows.note: The text gives a range across the bad-advice fine-tunes rather than assigning individual rates to domains. The evaluations use general prompts such as asking how to make a quick buck or what the model would do as ruler of the world.
rows.check: Should also link V7, since it gives effect size on an open 7B model. The range 11–31% is across three domains with no per-domain mapping in the text (Fig. 33). No EM rate is reported for the good-advice (D−) fine-tunes, so the matched benign control here is only the base model.

source_check.locator_found: §5, p. 10; Appendix I.2, Table 6 and Figure 33, p. 45.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated coherence of models fine-tuned on bad-advice datasets alongside EM.

conditions.value: bad advice: medical, financial, and sports

rows.note: The paper reports these coherence rates alongside the EM rates; it does not provide seed-based robustness results.
rows.check: The state should be observed rather than partial. Coherence stays at 80–88% versus 90% at baseline, which shows EM arises without much loss of coherence. The paper does not state whether EM scores were coherence-filtered (Betley judge prompts were used).

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Tracked EM during fine-tuning on the sports bad-advice dataset.
rows.measure: Onset of emergent misalignment during training
rows.value: By step ≈ 95, emergent misalignment appears; the loss has nearly converged.
rows.note: The text identifies this approximate point for the bad-sports-advice fine-tune.
rows.check: Onset is read off the dashed EM curve in Fig. 36 for the sports fine-tune only. The step-95 statement is in the Fig. 37 caption. There is no baseline, but checkpoint-5 gives an early-training reference.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix I.3, Figures 36–37, pp. 47–48; Figure 37 caption explicitly identifies approximately step 95.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Compared cosine similarity between contrastive evil behavior vectors and fine-tuning task vectors.

conditions.value: bad-advice fine-tunes and their good counterparts, plus control task vectors

rows.baseline: good counterparts and control task vectors
rows.value: Evil weight vectors are closer to misaligned task vectors than to good counterparts or control task vectors.
rows.note: This is evidence of geometric association, not a causal test that a direction mediates the behavior.
rows.check: Correlational cosine similarity in weight space, not mediation. The evil vectors come from fine-tunes on explicitly harmful advice or evil personality data (induced), compared against the bad-advice task vectors.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V5; cosine similarities establish geometric association, without testing whether intervention on the direction changes EM across fine-tunes.
source_check.problem: A correlational comparison cannot establish partial causal mediation under V5.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Compared cosine similarities among behavior weight vectors.

conditions.value: evil behavior vectors compared with control vectors

rows.measure: Cosine similarity among weight behavior vectors
rows.value: Evil weight vectors are more similar to each other than to the control; the authors describe the similarities as small.
rows.note: The paper interprets this as evidence of a shared evil direction, while noting that the cosine similarities are small.
rows.check: Similarity among evil weight vectors is above control but small, as the authors note. It is not a causal test.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V5; evil behavior vectors have small similarities exceeding the control comparison, without a causal mediation test.
source_check.problem: Small geometric similarities do not demonstrate that causal mediation is partial.
